Series::is_cpu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_cpu() const noexcept

What It Does¶

Returns true when this Series currently lives on the CPU platform, false when it lives on an accelerator.

It is a metadata read of platform() — platform() == Platform::CPU — and nothing else. It never transfers data, never probes what backends the machine supports, and cannot throw.

Placement is a property of each individual Series, decided when the tensor is created (zeros, make_series, and the rest build on CPU by default) and changed only by an explicit to(Platform) call. Two tensors in the same program can sit on different platforms, and most binary operations require both operands on the same one — is_cpu() (with its siblings is_cuda, is_mps, is_gpu) is how you check before combining or before reaching for direct host access.

is_cpu() answers “where is this tensor”. The different question “can this machine use backend X” is pluss::platform_available(p) — see Example 3.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true iff platform() == Platform::CPU.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_cpu() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. A freshly built Series is on the CPU; the four platform predicates for it read as one row of a truth table.

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "platform()=" << x.platform()
          << " is_cpu=" << x.is_cpu()
          << " is_gpu=" << x.is_gpu()
          << " is_cuda=" << x.is_cuda()
          << " is_mps=" << x.is_mps() << "\n";

Output¶

platform()=cpu is_cpu=true is_gpu=false is_cuda=false is_mps=false

Exactly one of is_cpu() and is_gpu() is ever true — they partition every Series. is_cuda() and is_mps() further pin which accelerator, and are both false here.

Example 2. to() moves the data; the predicates follow it. (Output from an Apple-Silicon host where MPS is available — a CUDA host or a CPU-only host reports its own platforms.)

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "before: is_cpu=" << x.is_cpu() << "\n";
auto m = x.to(pluss::pMPS);
std::cout << "on MPS: is_cpu=" << m.is_cpu() << " is_mps=" << m.is_mps() << "\n";
auto back = m.to(pluss::pCPU);
std::cout << "back:   is_cpu=" << back.is_cpu() << "\n";

Output¶

before: is_cpu=true
on MPS: is_cpu=false is_mps=true
back:   is_cpu=true

x, m, and back are three separate Series; to() never mutates the one it is called on.

Example 3. is_cpu() vs pluss::platform_available(pluss::pCPU) — two different questions.

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "x.is_cpu()                          = " << x.is_cpu() << "\n"
          << "platform_available(pCPU)  [machine] = " << pluss::platform_available(pluss::pCPU) << "\n"
          << "platform_available(pCUDA) [machine] = " << pluss::platform_available(pluss::pCUDA) << "\n"
          << "platform_available(pMPS)  [machine] = " << pluss::platform_available(pluss::pMPS) << "\n";

Output¶

x.is_cpu()                          = true
platform_available(pCPU)  [machine] = true
platform_available(pCUDA) [machine] = false
platform_available(pMPS)  [machine] = true

platform_available(pCPU) is always true; the accelerator entries depend on the host. Use platform_available to decide whether to move; use is_cpu() to check where a tensor already is.

Example 4. An undefined Series reports is_cpu() == true — because platform() defaults to Platform::CPU for a tensor with no storage.

pluss::Series undef;
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "defined()=" << undef.defined()
          << " is_cpu=" << undef.is_cpu()
          << " is_gpu=" << undef.is_gpu() << "\n";

Output¶

defined()=false is_cpu=true is_gpu=false

is_cpu() == true therefore does not guarantee a usable tensor — check defined() first if the Series might be uninitialized.

Example 5. Combining tensors from two platforms raises — the guard is_cpu() helps you place before this can happen.

auto a = pluss::series::zeros({2});                 // CPU
auto b = pluss::series::ones({2}).to(pluss::pMPS);  // MPS
try {
  auto c = a.add(b);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

add: expected all Series on same platform, got CPU and MPS

The fix is a.add(b.to(pluss::pCPU)) (or move a up to MPS) — decide with is_cpu() / is_mps() which direction to converge.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • is_cpu() is about this tensor’s current placement, not the machine’s capabilities. Use pluss::platform_available(p) for the latter.

  • An undefined Series reports is_cpu() == true. Pair with defined() when that matters.

  • Placement is per-Series. A binary op between a CPU tensor and an accelerator tensor raises; move one side with to() first.

  • The predicate never transfers data and never throws (noexcept) — it is free to call in a hot path.

Summary¶

is_cpu() reports whether a Series currently resides on the CPU:

  • platform() == Platform::CPU; the exact complement of is_gpu

  • per-tensor placement, set at creation, changed only by to(Platform)

  • distinct from pluss::platform_available(pCPU) (a machine capability, and always true)

  • true for an undefined Series — guard with defined()

See Also¶

  • Series::is_gpu: the exact negation — “on any accelerator”.

  • Series::is_cuda / Series::is_mps: the strict per-backend tests.

  • Series::platform(): the underlying Platform value these predicates read (cpu / cuda / mps).

  • Series::to: move a Series between platforms.
